newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Stampede on for Mexican pension funds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Stampede on for Mexican pension funds.

text.p: With a zeal reminiscent of the rush to buy Mexican banks in the early 1990s, a stampede is on in the financial community to grab a slice of Mexico's soon-to-be privatised national pension system.

From Europe, Chile and North America, suitors have flocked here to seek partners in a business that is not yet off the drawing board, but is expected to be an eventual goldmine for those who obtain an early lead.

The obstacles are stiff. In the presidential palace, Ernesto Zedillo has yet to put his signature to pension reform regulations that have been hammered out over recent months between government officials and private sector experts.
Hanging on the go-ahead are multi-million dollar deals struck between foreign banks, pension specialists and their Mexican counterparts.
WAITING FOR THE GREEN LIGHT

With less than four months to go before the targeted January 1, 1997 launch date for the private pension system, the government is unable to authorise any of the pension management firms, or Afores, until the regulations are ready.

Meanwhile, bankers are making business plans based on draft regulations and in doing so are being forced to break one of the golden rules of what is widely seen as an overmanned banking system -- hiring, rather than firing, staff.

The Afores are already shelling out cash to recruit thousands of sales and administrative staff. In the coming months, they will be trained in a business that for years has been in the hands of government accountants.
Adding to the cost, complex computer systems are being built to handle accounts for millions of Mexicans who entrust their nest eggs to the privately-run Afores.

"The time left for us is very short," said Juan Fernandez, head of a pension fund management firm set up by Mexican banking group Serfin, Citibank and its Chilean pension fund partner AFP Habitat. "Every day of the week will be important."
RACING AGAINST THE CLOCK
At a ceremony in mid-September to launch that fund, its owners made starkly clear the challenges ahead, though they also touted what they viewed as strong competitive advantages.

With about 100 working days left until the Afores are launched, they plan to hire and train 6,000 employees -- some 1,500 a month. The initial investment is planned for at least $70 million. At its launch, the Afore had not even been named.

On the other hand, Habitat has 15 years of experience running pension funds in Chile and is already a partner with Citibank in that South American market. Serfin, Mexico's third largest bank, has a nationwide branch network that will make capturing clients easier, officials said.

Other banking groups are just as tightly pressed. Spain's Banco Santander, that broke off an agreement to launch an Afore with Serfin in August, rushed to sign a letter of intent to set one up with Mexico's Grupo Financiero Inverlat just three weeks later.

On the plus side, Santander's Argentine pension subsidiary Origenes AFJP in September bought out its rival Activa-Anticipar in a deal that will make it the giant of that industry. That suggests it has the clout to make the business work in Mexico, Santander officials said.
THE ENVY OF ITS PEERS
With all the foreign experience available to its competitors, one Mexican banking giant already has a foothold that makes it the envy of the nascent industry.

Bancomer, owner of Mexico's second largest bank, currently holds some 35 percent of accounts in the government-run Retirement Savings System (SAR), and it hopes many workers will be more ready to keep their funds in the bank than shift them elsewhere.

But it has not rested on its laurels. Receiving a $47 million payment to link up with U.S. insurer Aetna and Chile's AFP Santa Maria, it has already surveyed potential clients on what they want from a pension fund.

It can also count on what officials say was $100 million invested in SAR-related computer systems over the last four years to set up what is expected to be one of the most sophisticated systems in the industry.
SOME 17 RUNNERS SEEN IN THE LINE-UP
According to industry expert Ernesto O'Farrill of consulting firm Bursametrica, some 17 Afores will seek approval to start business on January 1.
He estimates Bancomer's fund will achieve a 13 percent market share next year, while a partnership of Mexico's largest bank Banamex and Dutch insurer Aegon should garner 10 percent.

"It's very healthy that at the start of the race you see strong Afores. In a market like this which is starting from scratch, the natural tendency is to start with a large number," he told Reuters. "Then they will need to be more competitive and that will shrink the numbers over time."

He said he did not expect to see companies recouping their initial outlay for as long as seven years, but said the amount of workers eligible for pensions schemes in Mexico was bound to make it profitable. On the regulations front, there were several hurdles to overcome, however.

O'Farrill raised doubts about the smooth running of complex data banks at the central bank and the Social Security Institute set up to coordinate the pension contributions. He worried that account information could get lost, possibly undermining the credibility of the system.
BOWING TO POLITICAL PRESSURE
Analysts have also accused the government of bowing to political pressures in limiting Afore investments in the first year to mostly inflation-indexed, low-risk instruments.
"It's a total controversy," O'Farrill said. "You're going to hurt the whole system...there will be little competitiveness and you won't be able to see which are the best Afores."

In an interview, Daniel Lederman, vice-president of planning at the pension regulatory commission Consar said the investment restrictions were aimed at avoiding heavy losses. "It was a difficult change from a political point of view and we have to be careful there are (positive) returns."

Once Zedillo approves the regulations, he said, potential Afores will have some 20 days to apply for approval at Consar. Then they will face rigorous checks to ensure they are up to the task of running the accounts and are well capitalised.
The process "should be ready in January," he said. "Until we see when the regulations are published, we can't be sure."
